Only use this when you genuinely need all of it or the user asked for the whole file; otherwise read it in parts with offset and limit, or search it.

tools.name: ReportFindings
tools.description: Report code-review findings as a typed list so the host UI can render them. Use this only when the active code-review instructions tell you to report findings with this tool; otherwise follow whatever output format those instructions specify. When reporting a review's results, call it once with the verified findings ranked most-severe first (empty array if nothing survived verification) and do not also print the findings as text. When re-reporting after applying fixes (only if the apply instructions ask for it), set `outcome` on each finding to what actually happened.

level.description: Effort level the review ran at

findings.description: Verified findings, most-severe first; empty if none survived

file.description: Repo-relative path of the file the finding is in

short_summary.description: Compressed label for compact UI (≤60 chars): the claim alone, no rationale or consequence clause

category.description: Short kebab-case slug of the finding type, e.g. "correctness", "simplification", "efficiency", "test-coverage"

severity.description: Set when the review instructions ask for it. important: a bug the change adds or makes worse; pre_existing: a bug that was there before the change; nit: a minor issue

verdict.description: Set when a verify pass ran; absent on inline-only reviews

outcome.description: Set ONLY when re-reporting after applying fixes: what happened to this finding

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

delaySeconds.description: Seconds from now to wake up. Clamped to [60, 3600] by the runtime. Required unless `stop` is true.

reason.description: One short sentence explaining the chosen delay. Goes to telemetry and is shown to the user. Be specific. Required unless `stop` is true.

prompt.description: The /loop input to fire on wake-up. Pass the same /loop input verbatim each turn so the next firing re-enters the skill and continues the loop. For autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` instead (the dynamic-pacing variant, not the CronCreate-mode `<<autonomous-loop>>`). Required unless `stop` is true.

stop.description: Set to true to end the dynamic loop immediately instead of scheduling another wakeup. When true, all other fields are ignored and no further wakeups fire.

noop.description: true = nothing changed (you checked and there is nothing to report). false = something happened worth keeping (edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, surfaced a finding). Consecutive noop:true ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak. Required unless `stop` is true.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a listing from the system with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

skill.description: The name of a skill from the available-skills list. Do not guess names.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in a message from the system. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

query.description: Query to find deferred tools. Use "select:<tool_name>" for direct selection, or keywords to search.

max_results.description: Maximum number of results to return (default: 5)

tools.name: Write
tools.description:
Writes a file to the local filesystem, overwriting if one exists.

When to use: creating a new file, or fully replacing one you've already Read. Overwriting an existing file you haven't Read will fail. For partial changes, use Edit instead.

file_path.description: The absolute path to the file to write (must be absolute, not relative)

content.description: The content to write to the file

tools.name: mcp__t3-code__preview_act
tools.description: Act on the chosen tab. Target with `locator='aria-ref=<ref>'` from `preview_snapshot`; `x` and `y` go together. `timeoutMs` defaults to 15000. click: `button`, `clickCount` 1 to 3. type: literal `text`, `clear=true` replaces it. hover: shows menus or tooltips. select: `values` in one native <select>, by value or label; for a custom dropdown, click it open, then click the option. drag: `source` onto `target`. upload: absolute `paths` answer the file picker `preview_status` reports, [] cancels it, or a `locator` sets an <input type=file>. press: one `key`, such as 'Enter', with `modifiers`, to the focused element; click a field first to focus it. scroll: the tab, or one container with a locator; positive `deltaY` scrolls down, positive `deltaX` right.

tools.name: mcp__t3-code__preview_evaluate
tools.description: Run JavaScript in the page. It can change page state. Returns `{value}`, up to 64 KB. Needs your tab, or an unclaimed one. To read a tab the user drives, use `preview_snapshot`. Page tools write only on user request. Show results with `html_render`, never page tools.

tools.name: mcp__t3-code__preview_navigate
tools.description: Navigate the chosen tab. Pass `url` for a website, or `target:{kind:'environment-port',port}` for a dev server. Exactly one of `url` and `target`.

url.description: Website URL. Absolute http(s) URL, or a bare host (https; http for loopback). For public pages.
Website URL. Absolute http(s) URL, or a bare host (https; http for loopback).

path.description: Path, query, and fragment, such as /settings?tab=account.

tools.name: mcp__t3-code__preview_open
tools.description: Open a preview tab in this thread and show it. For a dev server, pass `target` instead of `url`. `open=false` keeps it in the background. Reuses your current tab unless `tabId` or `reuseExistingTab=false` says otherwise. Parallel subagents in one session must each use `reuseExistingTab=false`, then their own returned `tabId`.

url.description: First page URL. Absolute http(s) URL, or a bare host (https; http for loopback). Omit to open a blank tab.

open.description: Show the preview to the user. Default true. False for background only.

reuseExistingTab.description: Reuse `tabId`, or your current tab. Default true. False makes a new tab.

profileId.description: Profile id or name from preview_status, for a new tab. Default: the user's. A tab keeps its profile.

path.description: Path, query, and fragment, such as /settings?tab=account.

tools.name: mcp__t3-code__preview_resize
tools.description: Resize the chosen tab: {mode:'fill'}, {mode:'freeform',width,height}, or {mode:'preset',preset,orientation}. Changes CSS size only, not the user agent.

tools.name: mcp__t3-code__preview_snapshot
tools.description: Use it only when the current request asks for browser work, including checking an edit in the browser. Never use it unasked to verify your own edit, or to repeat a snapshot from an earlier turn. Works on a tab the user is driving. Returns page state, elements, diagnostics, and screenshot size. Target one element with `locator='aria-ref=<ref>'` from `accessibilityTree`, even in frames. Refs die on navigation, a new snapshot, or handoff. Text caps near 20 KB; on your own or an unclaimed tab, `preview_evaluate` reads more. To show a screenshot when asked: `save=true`, then embed ![alt](screenshotPath).

includeImage.description: Default false. True only to see the page.

tools.name: mcp__t3-code__request_secret
tools.description: Ask for secrets in a private card, one value per single-line input; never combine values in one. Open it, don't offer it. Returns one-use `secretRef`, or `delivery: "file"` a file read only in its command, e.g. `adb pair <ip:port> "$(cat <file>)"`. Asked how: call now. Sign-in link: `url`. Pasted secret for child/script: `value`. Never from an old thread.

url.description: Sign-in or setup page for the value. Shown as a button.

delivery.description: secretRef (default) for a T3 tool; file for a command.

secret.description: false shows the typed value, e.g. an email.

fields.description: Values only the user has, in one card, e.g. email + password, with delivery "file". Returns `files` by name.

value.description: Pasted in this thread; no card.

tools.name: mcp__t3-code__send_to_user
tools.description: Show the user a Markdown message in this thread, exactly as written, before your turn ends. Use it for content the user must read in full mid-turn, such as a draft, a code block, or what a question you are about to ask refers to. Don't repeat it in your reply.

tools.name: mcp__t3-code__t3_background_wait
tools.description: Keep this thread in Working while background work runs. Pass its task ID once started. Not for work left running (dev server, watcher). `waiting=false` clears. Doesn't stop tasks.

tools.name: DeferredToolPlaceholder
tools.description: Reserved placeholder that keeps deferred tool loading active; never call this tool.

tools.name: mcp__t3-code__t3_preview_close
tools.description: Close one preview tab this thread owns. Use it on a tab you opened for your own check when you finish.

The hidden browser seems to be signing in as the environment's owner rather than the e2e QA user, which would explain the 404 from a workspace mismatch. That's fine in production with a single owner, but I'd rather not depend on auto sign-in at all. Passing the caller's session cookies to the hidden browser would make the preview see exactly what the requesting user sees, which seems like the right design. I'm also wondering whether the browser's sign-in is working at all, since the "not found" page doesn't tell me whether it was signed in.

I'm deciding to pass the caller's session cookies into lookAt, reading them via next/headers in the chat route and threading them through Run, since that keeps the hidden browser's view tied to the requesting user. For the Playwright side, I'd add them to the shared context per call, while I'm leaning toward skipping cookies on desktop because the Electron session already holds the owner's cookies. I'm also wondering whether reading cookies inside the streaming execute would still be within request scope, so I'm considering reading them up front in the route instead.

Next I'm planning to pass the caller's session cookies through to the hidden browser, gathering the `sb-` cookies once in the route and adding them to the Playwright context before navigating. The cookie domain should work against the loopback address since I'd set it by URL, and Supabase's cookie names come from the Supabase URL rather than the app host, so the names should match. The remaining worry is that if the hidden browser refreshes an expired access token, it could rotate the refresh token out from under the owner's real browser session.

I'm accepting the risk of the hidden browser refreshing the owner's token here, since the token was just refreshed on this request and should last about an hour. I'll also pass the caller's cookies through in the dev-look path.
The hidden browser used the server owner's account rather than the test user's, which is why it returned "not found". I'm changing the preview to pass through the caller's session cookies instead.

content.thinking:
I'm working out how Tailwind's `@theme` tokens end up in CSS: they come out as `:root` custom properties using `light-dark()`, and the utilities reference them through `var()`. My thought is that unregistered custom properties keep the token sequence, so `light-dark()` resolves at the point of use against the element's `color-scheme`, which means a wrapper with `colorScheme: dark` should flip it.

I'm checking whether ThemePreference overriding `data-theme` on the html element could break the wrapper's `colorScheme: dark` cascade, and whether Tailwind might register these colors with `@property`. The screenshot still shows light, so something else may be resolving `light-dark()` earlier than I expect. A more reliable route would be to set `data-theme` directly in the preview page, though ThemePreference could overwrite it after hydration, so the ordering matters.

I'm weighing a different approach: have ThemePreference skip itself on the draft-card preview path, and instead render a small client component that forces `data-theme` to the requested theme in an effect. That would avoid the hydration race.

content.text:
All three changes are built and committed on `t3/improve-artifact-preview`. The QA app is running from this branch at http://127.0.0.1:3100, and I've opened its Settings page for you.

**What changed:**

1. **The designer gets your words.** It used to see only a short summary written by the chat model. Now it also gets your last messages, thinks a bit harder, and the example prompts no longer carry the long design paragraph. That paragraph is also why your Scalable page came out light while the app is dark.
2. **Widget building blocks.** There's now a big number that shrinks to fit, a list that shows the rows that fit plus "+N more", a progress bar, and columns that can't overlap. The designer is told to build from these first, so a plain "show my portfolio" should look right without describing pixels.
3. **It looks at what it built.** After building, Moneo renders the draft in a hidden browser with your real data:
   - widgets at S, M, L and XL in dark, plus M in light;
   - pages at desktop width and phone width.

   It sends the designer the screenshots plus a list of problems it measured: cut-off text, overlaps, text too small, sideways scrolling on a phone, ignoring dark mode. The designer replies "OK" or sends a fixed version, at most twice.

**What I checked:** I made a test card copying the bugs from your Scalable widget (donut on top of the list, rows cut off, a huge number). The measuring caught every one of them and reported nothing on a card made from the new blocks. Each check took about 4 seconds. Tests, lint, typecheck and the production build all pass.

**How to test:**
1. In the QA app's Settings → AI access, sign in with ChatGPT or paste an API key. Its built-in key is a fake one that always gets rejected.
2. Go to AI → Artifacts and ask in plain words, like you did before: "a nice view of my Scalable with a pie chart, cash included". Then ask for a Home card. The QA data is made up, so ask about things it has.
3. Look at the card at each size in the Home card tab.

Each build now takes longer: about 5 seconds of screenshots plus one extra designer reply per look.

**Untested parts:**
- **The desktop app's hidden window** isn't tested in a real desktop build yet. Its bridge route has tests, but I haven't packaged the app.
- **ChatGPT sign-in in QA** may not complete on port 3100. If it doesn't, the API key route works.
- **The "N" circle in screenshots** is the dev-mode badge from the QA server. Production doesn't show it.

Tell me how it looks, and I'll open the PR once you're happy.
